title: Countdown and Stopwatch: Laps, Background Timing, Sleep Limits
description: The countdown recomputes remaining from a deadline, so throttling adds no drift; the stopwatch splits laps on a monotonic clock. Presets, pause, sleep limits.
content:
The site's countdown and stopwatch tool puts two timers on one page: the upper half is a countdown that runs against a deadline, the lower half is a stopwatch that records elapsed time. On load the countdown reads 05:00 and the inputs are prefilled with 5 minutes 0 seconds; the stopwatch reads 00:00.0, and both panels are in the Ready state.

The countdown panel runs from top to bottom: state badge, dial, four presets, minute and second inputs, Start / Pause / Reset, the sound checkbox, a status bar and the hint “Keep this page open while timing.”; the stopwatch panel is a readout, four buttons and a lap list. Both readouts carry role="timer" and aria-live="off".

1. On opening the page: 5 minutes by default, two panels with one job each

Countdown stateReadoutPrimary buttonPause buttonMinutes / seconds and presets
ReadyCurrent duration (default 05:00)StartDisabledEditable
RunningRemaining time, rounded up to the secondStart (disabled)AvailableDisabled
PausedFrozen at the moment of pauseResumeDisabledEditable; any change returns to Ready
Time is up00:00Start againDisabledEditable

2. Setting a duration: four presets, or your own minutes and seconds

The four presets are 1, 5, 15 and 25 minutes. When the current duration exactly matches a preset, that button carries the pressed state aria-pressed="true"; on first load that is 5 minutes. Clicking a preset sets the minutes field to that number, clears the seconds, and resets the countdown to the new duration.

You can also edit the two inputs directly: minutes accept integers from 0–999, seconds accept integers from 0–59, and their sum must be above zero. If any condition fails, the readout becomes “—”, the Start button is disabled, and the status bar shows the same error: “Enter whole minutes (0–999) and seconds (0–59), with a total above zero.”

  • Decimals don’t work: 1.5 minutes is not a whole number, and an empty value or letters fail the same way.
  • Out-of-range values don’t work: 1000 minutes or 60 seconds both exceed the input’s maximum.
  • 0 minutes 0 seconds doesn’t work: the total must be above zero, and the shortest valid duration is 1 second.

Changing the duration resets a paused or finished countdown back to Ready and clears the error message, but it does not press Start for you: adjusting the duration only sets a new starting point, and you still have to click Start once more.

3. Start, pause, resume: the button labels follow the state

After you click Start the state becomes Running, the Start button is disabled and the Pause button is available; the minutes and seconds inputs and the four presets are disabled at the same time, so the duration cannot be changed mid-run. The dial’s progress arc is drawn from the remaining proportion, and the readout counts down in whole seconds.

Click Pause and the remaining time freezes at that second, the state becomes Paused, the primary button changes from Start to Resume, and the status bar also reads Paused. The readout does not change while paused; Resume sets a new deadline from that remaining time instead of counting the paused interval as elapsed.

When the countdown reaches zero the state becomes Time is up, the primary button becomes Start again, and the readout stays at 00:00; pressing it once more returns to the full duration and starts over. If the inputs have been left at invalid values, Reset first repairs them from the last valid duration and then resets: if the timer last stopped at 0 minutes 30 seconds, for example, and the fields were changed to 0 and 0, Reset restores 0 and 30.

4. Why switching to the background doesn’t slow it down: a deadline, not a decrement

Internally the countdown does one thing: when it starts it records a deadline (the current moment plus the remaining milliseconds), and every later readout recomputes the remaining time as the deadline minus the current moment, clamped at zero. Nothing subtracts 100 milliseconds per heartbeat, so a missed callback never turns into accumulated error. The heartbeat fires every 100 milliseconds, but it only redraws; for display the remaining milliseconds are rounded up to the second, and the readout is still decided by the wall clock.

Jump a 5-minute countdown 65 seconds ahead in Chromium’s fake clock and the panel shows 03:55 straight away, without replaying the 650 heartbeats of those 65 seconds. Throttling, dropped frames and backgrounding change when it redraws, not how much time has passed. To check which date a particular instant corresponds to, you can put the millisecond timestamp into the timestamp converter and compare.

But 100 milliseconds is only the redraw cadence, not a precision promise. MDN’s setInterval documentation states plainly that the actual time between two callbacks can be longer than the configured delay; browsers also throttle background tabs: Chrome 88’s intensive throttling stretches the check interval to once a minute when several conditions hold at once: the page has been hidden for more than five minutes, the timer chain count is at least 5, the page has been silent for at least 30 seconds and WebRTC is not in use. That does not affect the countdown, but it does make this page unsuitable for measurements that need evenly spaced samples.

5. Background, hidden tabs and system sleep: three different kinds of stop

While the page is hidden the browser may throttle the timer, and the readout can sit on an old value; the page listens for visibilitychange and redraws as soon as the document is visible again, so what you see on return is the latest remaining time computed from the deadline. When the page enters the back/forward cache, leaving clears the heartbeat and closes the audio context, and on return, if pageshow’s persisted is true, it restarts the heartbeat and redraws immediately; the cache keeps the deadline in memory, so the remaining time still counts from the original deadline.

During system sleep the countdown reads the wall clock from Date.now(): the system time crosses the deadline, so after waking the remaining time is 0 and the panel may show Time is up straight away. The stopwatch reads the monotonic clock from performance.now(), which advances at a constant rate and is not affected by manual system clock changes, but whether that clock keeps running while the system is suspended is not consistent across platforms and browsers. The page does not compensate for sleep, and “how long it slept” should not be treated as a quantity that can be exactly recomputed.

Sound has a similar boundary: the end chime is triggered when a redraw observes Time is up, and if the page is hidden at that moment and audio is suspended, the sound may only arrive once you return to the page. When you need a reminder on the dot, a separate system alarm is the safer choice; the world clock can help you confirm whether the device time is trustworthy.

6. The stopwatch: tenths, accumulated pauses and lap splits

The stopwatch computes elapsed time as “accumulated plus the current run”: Start records an origin, Pause adds the run to the accumulator and clears the origin, and Resume records a new origin. The readout floors milliseconds to a tenth of a second, so it shows in a format like 00:03.4, where the last digit stands for 0.1 seconds.

Clicking Lap records two numbers at once: the total elapsed since the start, and the difference from the previous lap, which is the split. The list puts the newest entry on top and pads the number to two digits; every row also carries accessible text for the lap, the split and the total.

Once the stopwatch is paused, Lap is disabled and the readout stops; after Resume it continues from the accumulated value. Reset clears the accumulator, the origin and the whole list, the readout returns to 00:00.0, and the empty-list hint appears again.

Stopwatch stateReadoutStart buttonPause / LapLap list
Ready00:00.0StartBoth disabledEmpty hint
RunningCounts up in tenths of a secondStart (disabled)Both availableAppends, newest on top
PausedFrozen at the moment of pauseResumeBoth disabledKept
After reset00:00.0StartBoth disabledCleared

7. The chime: why the audio is prepared when you click Start

Sound is off by default. Once Sound when finished is ticked, the page creates or reuses the audio context inside that same click on Start and tries to resume it: browser autoplay policies restrict scripts from starting audio without a user gesture, and MDN’s autoplay guide treats script-initiated playback as subject to the policy.

The end chime is three short sine tones at 660, 880 and 660 Hz, about 0.24 seconds apart, with the volume rising quickly and then decaying. There are three conditions for it to fire: the checkbox is ticked, the audio context exists, and the state is running; miss one and it stays silent.

If resuming the audio context throws, the status bar shows “Sound is unavailable in this browser. The visual alert is active.” and timing is unaffected. The audio context is closed when the page is left; after a restore from the back/forward cache, the next click on Start prepares it again.

8. Refresh and closing the page: neither timer is saved

The state of the countdown and the stopwatch exists only in the current page’s memory; the code never writes the remaining time, the duration or the laps to localStorage or sessionStorage. A refresh, a closed tab, a different device or cleared site data all return both timers to their initial values: 05:00 and 00:00.0.

The page says as much itself: “Keep this page open while timing.” That is the real boundary of this implementation. For a deadline hours or days away, a system alarm, a phone timer or a calendar reminder is more reliable; to count the days between two dates use the date difference calculator, and to schedule by working days use the workday calculator — they work on dates rather than on a running timer.

9. Boundaries and limits: treat it as a visible short-duration timer

On precision, the countdown shows whole seconds only and the stopwatch shows tenths only; even with a 100-millisecond heartbeat, that does not mean the readout can reflect differences smaller than 100 milliseconds. MDN’s Date.now and Performance.now documentation both note that browsers may reduce timestamp precision according to privacy settings. Changing the system clock by hand also makes the countdown jump; the stopwatch depends on the monotonic clock, so a system-clock change does not affect it, but device sleep, the browser freezing the page or the process being killed can all break that continuity, and the exact behaviour depends on the platform and browser (whether the monotonic clock keeps running during sleep, for instance, is not consistent between implementations).

Neither path can keep running in the background or sync across tabs: open several tabs and you have several unrelated timers. In practice, decide first whether you need to see the readout or to be reminded on the dot: the former suits this page, the latter belongs to a system-level reminder, or at least keep the page open and run it once with sound on. The page can guarantee that while it is visible it shows the remaining time against the deadline and pauses and resumes as operated; the chime sounds only when Sound when finished is ticked and the audio context is available; it does not guarantee that timing continues after the page is closed.

faqs.q: Does the countdown keep going when I switch to another tab?
faqs.a: It keeps counting against the deadline, but a background page may be throttled by the browser, so the readout is not necessarily refreshed on time. The page redraws immediately when the document becomes visible again, so what you see on return is the remaining time computed from the deadline, not the frame you left behind.

faqs.q: Why does the button read Start again once it reaches 00:00?
faqs.a: That is the Time is up state of the state machine. Remaining is zero, the primary button becomes Start again, and pressing it starts over from the full duration; to go back to Ready without starting, press Reset.

faqs.q: Why does changing the duration after a pause return to Ready?
faqs.a: Editing either input or clicking a preset resets the countdown to the new duration, the state returns to Ready, and the old paused progress is discarded. To keep that progress, do not change the duration while paused.

faqs.q: How are the stopwatch splits calculated?
faqs.a: Each lap records the total elapsed since the start, and the split is that total minus the previous total. The list puts the newest entry on top, pads the number to two digits, and shows both split and total to a tenth of a second.

faqs.q: What if there is no sound at the end?
faqs.a: First check that Sound when finished is ticked, then that the browser allowed audio when you pressed Start. If resuming the audio context fails, the status bar reports that sound cannot be played; audio in a hidden tab may also be suspended, so the sound arrives only once the page is visible.

faqs.q: Is the timer still there after a refresh?
faqs.a: No. Countdown and stopwatch state live only in the current page’s memory; nothing is written to localStorage or sessionStorage. A refresh, a closed tab or a different device returns both to 05:00 and 00:00.0. That is exactly what the page hint Keep this page open while timing refers to.

Autoplay guide for media and Web Audio APIs

focus: The countdown computes the remaining time from a deadline, and a 100-millisecond heartbeat only redraws, so background throttling and missed callbacks do not accumulate error; the stopwatch accumulates elapsed time on a monotonic clock and records lap splits. The article also covers pause, start again, lap timing, the chime and back/forward cache behaviour, plus the real boundaries: no persistence, system sleep and audio in a hidden tab.
